title: What Leaders Can Learn From a Snow Day
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Prompted by a real winter storm, this piece uses the familiar 'snow day' dilemma facing schools and organizations as a case study in decision communication. It argues that the specific decision to open or close matters less than whether leaders clearly explain the information and reasoning behind it, since reasonable people will disagree with either choice. The piece contrasts vague, unexplained announcements with transparent ones that share the criteria and information considered, arguing the latter builds trust regardless of outcome. It closes by generalizing this principle beyond weather calls to any decision where reasonable people might disagree.
points: The decision itself in close-call situations often matters less than how transparently it's communicated.
Reasonable people will disagree with either choice, so unexplained decisions erode trust while explained ones preserve it.
Sharing the information and criteria behind a call builds long-term credibility even amid disagreement.
The principle is generalized beyond weather decisions to any close call leaders make.
quotes: What erodes trust isn’t the decision. It’s when people feel the decision was made carelessly or without understanding the impact it has on others.
The best leaders offer people an inside view about the decision itself and the process used to make it.
This transparency builds long-term credibility even when people disagree with the choice.
Anytime leaders face a choice where reasonable people might disagree, the transparency of their thinking matters more than the outcome.
Great leaders spend less time agonizing over the right decision and more time being clear about how they are going about making it.
More often than not, credibility springs from the transparency of the process, not the outcome.
